topline.text: Labour's conference in Liverpool (running to tomorrow) produced two lines with real classroom weight: new vocational GCSEs alongside the traditional set from 2029, and a demand that schools 'go further' than existing RSHE teaching to shift the wider culture on misogyny.

The OECD published its Education at a Glance 2026 report today, with this year's special focus on teacher shortages — previous editions have flagged England as having one of the OECD's worst teacher attrition rates.

diary.text: Labour's annual conference in Liverpool closes; the PE and sport premium digital expenditure return is also due by 5pm the same day.
NEU national executive reconvenes to decide whether and when to relaunch the paused strike ballot.

sections.heading: Labour conference: two lines for schools

items.body: Education secretary Lucy Powell used her conference speech to confirm vocational GCSEs — covering subjects like construction, child development and business — sitting alongside traditional GCSEs from as early as September 2029. She rejected the 'dumbing down' charge, calling them 'very hard subjects' with real maths and problem-solving content.
items.action: Four years out, but worth a mention to your curriculum/options lead as a future pathway for pupils the current GCSE offer doesn't serve well.

items.lede: Schools told to 'go further' on misogyny.
items.body: Powell said schools must move beyond this year's RSHE strategy and embed healthy relationships 'into every part of school life, not just RSHE lessons', including teaching on deepfakes, image-based abuse and online harassment. Her line: 'We simply cannot just teach our way out of misogyny.'
items.action: Worth checking with your PSHE/RSHE lead that deepfakes and image-based abuse are explicitly covered, not folded into a generic online-safety unit.

box.text: of England's teachers left the profession in the most recent year the OECD measured — over three times the rate in France or Ireland. That was last year's Education at a Glance; this year's edition, published today with a fresh focus on teacher shortages, will show whether the gap has moved. Figure unconfirmed for the 2026 edition at time of writing.
